questions.q: Why does a RAG pipeline retrieve small chunks instead of handing a model the whole document set?
options: Because chunking is required by the Python language itself
Because whole documents cannot be stored in a vector database under any circumstances
Because chunking removes the need for any embedding model
Because retrieval works by finding the few passages that actually answer a question and using only those
questions.explain: The lesson explains that RAG retrieves only the small passages closest to a question, instead of handing the model the entire document set, which is why documents need to be split into chunks worth retrieving individually.

questions.q: What does the lesson's loader keep alongside each document's text, and why?
options: The file's creation date, because citations need a timestamp
The file's path, because Lesson 5's citations point back to it
Nothing else is kept — only the raw text matters
The file's byte size, for compression purposes
questions.explain: The loader keeps each file's path alongside its text specifically because that path is what citations in Lesson 5 point back to.

questions.q: In what order does RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter try its separators, per this lesson?
options: Only at the word level, never at paragraph or sentence boundaries
Randomly, with no defined order
Paragraph breaks first, then line breaks, then sentence and word boundaries, falling back to a mid-sentence cut only as a last resort
Mid-sentence cuts first, then paragraph breaks
questions.explain: The splitter tries cleaner separators first — paragraph breaks, then lines, then sentence/word boundaries — and only cuts mid-sentence when nothing cleaner fits inside the chunk size.

questions.q: What problem does chunk overlap solve?
options: It prevents a sentence spanning a chunk boundary from being lost in both halves
It removes the need for a vector database entirely
It makes chunks smaller so retrieval runs faster
It eliminates the need for chunk metadata
questions.explain: Without overlap, a sentence straddling a chunk boundary is cut in half with neither chunk carrying the full idea; overlap repeats the tail of one chunk as the head of the next so the passage stays whole somewhere.

questions.q: Which three fields does each chunk carry per this lesson, and what reads chunk_id back out?
options: text, author, and date — author is read back by Lesson 5
embedding, score, and rank — score is read back by Lesson 4 itself
text, source, and chunk_id — chunk_id is read back by Lesson 6's evaluation
Only text is kept; source and chunk_id are discarded after chunking
questions.explain: Each chunk carries text, source, and chunk_id; the lesson states that chunk_id (along with source) is read back by Lesson 6's evaluation to check whether retrieval pulled the correct chunk.
